title: Gentle Words and Open Hearts
overview: A collection of short sayings about how we speak, how we take correction, and why an honest, humble life is worth more than wealth.

parts.label: Words that heal or wound (vv. 1-2, 4, 7, 23, 28)
parts.note: A calm reply can cool someone's anger while a sharp one feeds it, so a wise person weighs an answer before giving it. Calling kind speech a "tree of life" means it renews and strengthens people, while twisted, cruel words can crush a person's spirit.

parts.label: Nothing hidden from God (vv. 3, 8-9, 11, 26, 29)
parts.note: If even the depths of the realm of the dead lie open before the LORD (the Hebrew names this place Sheol and Abaddon), then human hearts certainly do. That is why offerings from someone living cruelly are rejected while an honest person's simple prayer is welcomed: the life behind the worship matters more than the ritual.

parts.label: Accepting correction (vv. 5, 10, 12, 31-32)
parts.note: Brushing off a parent's or teacher's correction is treated as foolish and even self-harming, as if you did not value your own life. The warning that such a person faces death most likely points to the ruin someone heads toward when they let no one warn them.

parts.label: Better a little with love (vv. 6, 16-17, 27)
parts.note: An animal fattened in a stall was rich meat saved for feasts, and a plate of greens was a poor person's meal, yet a simple dinner among people who love each other beats a banquet full of hatred. Wealth gained through greed or bribes is said to bring trouble on the whole household.

parts.label: The inner life shows (vv. 13-15, 30)
parts.note: A glad heart lights up the face, and deep sorrow can drain a person's strength. A bright face and good news are said to reach right into the bones, an old way of saying they refresh a person through and through.

parts.label: Humility and the upward path (vv. 18-25, 33)
parts.note: Patience, advice from others and steady effort clear the way, while hot temper, pride and laziness choke it like a thorn hedge. Boundary stones marked a family's land and widows were easy targets for land grabs, so the LORD guarding them shows he sides with the vulnerable, and the chapter ends by saying humility comes before honor.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether sayings like these about treasure and safety for the righteous are promises God guarantees or general patterns of how life usually works, with many exceptions.
think: When has someone's gentle or harsh words changed the direction of a moment for you, and what made the difference?
